mediaItem.itemTitle: Maggie Freleng with Talalelei TJ Edwards
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction with Maggie Freeling tells the story of Tala Lele Edwards Jr., known as TJ, who was wrongfully convicted in 2004 for the murder of his godson, one-year-old Derek, in Anchorage, Alaska.  TJ was accused of Shaken Baby Syndrome based on the triad of injuries: brain bleeding, swollen brain, and bleeding in the eyes, despite no external trauma.  The podcast details TJ's background, his strong family values, and the events leading to Derek's death while in TJ's care.  Despite TJ's adamant innocence and the fact that Derek had been sick and had a scratch on his head prior to the incident, police focused solely on TJ as the suspect, ignoring other potential causes and evidence.  The episode highlights the racial bias TJ felt as a Polynesian man during the investigation and the devastating impact of the wrongful conviction on him and his family, as he served 14 years for a crime he maintains he did not commit.

featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: One-year-old Derek was in the care of his godfather, TJ, while Derek's mother, Melissa, was at work. TJ noticed Derek was not breathing and rushed him to the hospital. Derek died at the hospital, and doctors determined he had brain bleeding and swelling.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Implied to be the "triad" of injuries (brain bleeding, swelling, eye bleeding) considered indicative of Shaken Baby Syndrome at the time, and TJ being the last adult caregiver. The prosecution seems to have emphasized TJ's size as a Polynesian man, suggesting he could have violently shaken the child.

keyQuotesRaw: TJ: "When they say guilty, I was shocked. And what made it real for me was my mom. She started building out crying and I looked back at her and I just seen her just like getting weak and just everybody trying to pick her up. I hate reliving that memory. That was the one that made me all stuck in here." - Illustrates the shock and emotional impact of the guilty verdict.

Detective (paraphrased): "TJ, man, look how big you are. Like, if I was a kid and you over here, like, shaking me, I would be in the same position Derek's hand." - Shows the biased and presumptive line of questioning based on TJ's physical appearance and racial stereotype.

TJ: "Polynesians were getting into altercations with the police and stuff like that at that time and we were definitely being frowned upon as far as growing up here with the law against, you know, the Poly community back then." - Highlights the racial context and potential bias in law enforcement interactions with the Polynesian community in Anchorage.
systemicIssuesRaw: Flawed understanding and misdiagnosis of Shaken Baby Syndrome at the time.
Confirmation bias in police investigations, focusing solely on SBS and TJ as the suspect, ignoring other evidence.
Potential racial bias within the justice system against Polynesian individuals in Anchorage.
Lack of trust in law enforcement within the Polynesian community, stemming from negative past experiences.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Re-evaluation of cases based on outdated or flawed medical diagnoses like SBS "triad."
Addressing racial bias in policing and the justice system.
Improved investigative practices to avoid tunnel vision and consider all evidence.
personalNarrativeRaw: TJ's personal narrative emphasizes his love for family and children, contrasting with the accusation of harming a child.
The wrongful conviction caused immense emotional distress and trauma for TJ and his family, particularly his mother.
He lost 14 years of his life due to this wrongful conviction.
The experience deepened his distrust of law enforcement and the justice system.
